strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: the reliability of model stitching as a functional similarity metric, building constructively on recent critiques of task loss matching (TLM) [2, 19, 40].

The proposed FuLA objective (Eq. 5) is simple, clearly formulated, and well-motivated: it combines stitch-level feature alignment (structural hint) with task-agnostic 'functional hints' propagated through frozen end-model layers, explicitly avoiding output-level cues that can be exploited.

The experimental design is thoughtful — the adversarial training, shortcut learning, and class-subset settings are cleverly constructed testbeds where task-based stitching can be shown to fabricate or overlook alignment (e.g., SLM/TLM hallucinating non-robust accuracy when stitching between non-robust models).

Substantial empirical coverage: three architectures (ResNet18/34 and a no-residual variant), two datasets, multiple stitching depths, cross-layer 9x9 stitching grids, and a useful methodological clarification that DM as originally implemented is unfairly disadvantaged (Fig. 3).
Honest limitations section, and the distinction between TLM and SLM (footnote 1) is a genuinely useful observation for the community.
weaknesses: The central claim — that FuLA is a 'more reliable' functional similarity metric — is difficult to support because, as the authors concede, there is no ground truth for functional similarity. The evidence is largely qualitative: plots are inspected for 'smooth interpolation' and 'intuitive' behavior, which is an informal criterion. There is no quantitative validation against a known positive/negative control pair where ground truth is available by construction (e.g., identical model vs. shuffled-label model), beyond the random-chance sanity check.

Originality is modest: FuLA is essentially feature distillation (Fitnets hints [39]) transplanted into the stitching framework, and the authors themselves trace the idea of function consistency to KD work [27]. The contribution is a new application/setting rather than a new method or a new theoretical understanding of functional similarity.

Some results are inconvenient for the narrative and are interpreted post-hoc: Hint outperforms FuLA in the non-robust-to-robust configuration at deeper layers, and both Hint and FuLA report random-chance performance at the penultimate layer (Sec. 3.1) — the latter looks like an artifact of the method itself, yet it is reframed as 'more accurately detecting' dissimilarity. A stronger analysis (e.g., why does FuLA fail at layer 9?) would be needed.

The reliability of FuLA is primarily argued via instability of TLM/SLM, creating a somewhat circular comparison: FuLA is judged by the same stitched-accuracy quantity that task-based stitching is criticized for optimizing. The paper would benefit from additional independent validation (e.g., correlation with other metrics, behavioral probes, transfer tests), especially since CKA is only briefly compared.

Evaluation hygiene is thin: no error bars, seeds, or variance reporting for the stitching results; conclusions often rest on visual inspection of dense multi-panel figures (Figs. 4-5, 8) that are hard to read at print resolution.

Scope is narrow: only small CNNs on CIFAR-10 and a 10-class low-resolution ImageNet subset, classification only. The abstract mentions introducing 'a new testbed,' but the shortcut setting is the closest thing and its implications are not thoroughly analyzed (e.g., why FuLA exploits location shortcuts only in cross-dataset stitching).

Several design choices lack ablation or justification in the main text: uniform weighting of hints, the norm normalization in Eq. 5, number of functional hints, and the sensitivity of results to these choices (Fig. 11 is the only probe, and it is coarse).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and relevant problem: the reliability of model stitching as a proxy for functional similarity, following up on the recent DM-vs-TLM debate (Balogh & Jelasity).

The proposed FuLA objective is clearly formalized (Eq. 5), sensibly motivated via the function-consistency view, and the decision to exclude output-level cues to avoid task-cue leakage is a reasonable design choice.

The experimental design is thoughtful: three targeted testbeds (adversarial training, shortcut learning, cross-layer stitching) are constructed to stress specific failure modes (fabricated alignment, overfitting to cues), and the disentangling of SLM vs. TLM is a useful clarification.

The paper is honest about limitations (lack of ground truth, restriction to image classification), and the supplementary material extends results to multiple architectures (ResNet18/34, plain CNN), improving reproducibility.
Some empirical findings are interesting, e.g., that directionality persists under task-agnostic alignment, and the penultimate-layer dissimilarity analysis combining CKA and FuLA.
weaknesses: Limited originality: FuLA is essentially feature-hint distillation (Fitnets; Romero et al.) applied through the frozen end-model of a stitching setup, a combination already foreshadowed by function-consistent distillation (Liu et al.) and DM initialization. The methodological delta over existing stitching objectives is small and mostly reduces to adding distillation terms at post-stitch layers.

The central claim — that FuLA is 'a more reliable metric' for functional similarity — is not convincingly established. Without ground truth, the evidence rests on qualitative judgments ('behaves more stably', 'smoothly interpolates'), and the paper's own shortcut experiments admit FuLA is also susceptible to exploiting shortcuts, which directly undercuts the reliability claim.

The evaluation scale is narrow: CIFAR-10 and a 10-class low-resolution ImageNet subset, ResNet-family CNNs only, small models. No modern architectures (ViTs), no larger datasets, and no quantitative statistical treatment (error bars, seeds, significance) supporting the comparative claims.

The hyperparameter sensitivity of the FuLA objective (weights C, number/depth of functional hints) is underexplored; Fig. 11 shows conclusions change with hint weighting, but no principled guidance or ablation over these choices is provided for the main experiments.

Reported anomalies are noted but not resolved, e.g., the random-chance performance of both Hint and FuLA at the penultimate layer in the non-robust-to-robust configuration, and cases where Hint outperforms FuLA are reinterpreted post hoc ('may indicate functional misalignment') rather than analyzed.

Presentation quality is below the bar for the main track: several figures (Figs. 4, 5, 8, 10) are dense, small, and difficult to read, making it hard to verify the claimed trends; key comparisons are often described only in prose.

The added computational cost of FuLA (backpropagating through multiple frozen end-model layers vs. the closed-form DM solution) is acknowledged only in a footnote and is never quantified against the benefit.

Significance is moderate: the practical utility of a 'more reliable' stitching metric is demonstrated only within the authors' own controlled testbeds, and the paper does not show downstream value (e.g., changed conclusions in a known application of stitching).

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated weakness in existing model stitching settings (SLM/TLM can 'fabricate' alignment by exploiting task cues, while stitch-level DM ignores downstream functional behavior) and proposes a simple, principled remedy (FuLA) that aligns latents through the frozen downstream layers of the end model in a task-agnostic manner.

The experimental design is thoughtful: the authors construct controlled testbeds (adversarial training, injected shortcuts, label/class shift, cross-layer stitching) where pathologies of task-based stitching can be exposed, rather than relying solely on aggregate numbers.

The empirical coverage is broad for the scope: CIFAR-10 and LS-ImageNet-10, three architectures (ResNet18, ResNet34, residual-free variant), multiple stitching configurations (α values, same- vs cross-task, 9 stitching locations, 9×9 cross-layer grids), with full supplementary results that support the main conclusions.

The paper makes useful clarifying observations, e.g., that DM as originally implemented underperforms due to sample count and running batch statistics (Fig. 3), and that directionality persists even under task-agnostic alignment (Sec. 3.3), which is a substantive finding for the stitching literature.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: training details, optimizer settings, initialization (Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse), AutoAttack configuration, and shortcut constructions are all documented in the appendix, and limitations are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: The central claim that FuLA is 'a more reliable metric of functional similarity' is not conclusively supported because there is no ground truth for functional similarity. The validation is largely by showing FuLA behaves 'more intuitively' in the designed testbeds, which risks circularity: the criteria (i)-(ii) in Sec. 1 are the authors' own hypotheses, and the experiments are designed to confirm them. Higher stitching accuracy under FuLA is not by itself evidence of reliability.

The paper does not fully rule out that FuLA also fabricates alignment in subtler ways. In Sec. 3.1 there are cases where Hint outperforms FuLA and both report random-chance performance at the penultimate layer for the non-robust-to-robust setting; the interpretation offered ('may indicate functional misalignment that Hint fails to detect') is post-hoc and unverified. A systematic analysis of FuLA's own failure modes is missing.

Originality is modest: FuLA essentially transfers hint-based feature distillation (FitNets [39]) and function-consistency ideas from KD [27] into the stitching setting. The contribution is a new optimality condition and an empirical study rather than a fundamentally new method; the delta over Hint (structural term + deeper functional hints) is incremental.

Scope is narrow relative to the framing: only CNNs on CIFAR-10 and a 10-class low-resolution ImageNet subset. The abstract and conclusion make broad claims about functional similarity evaluation in AI, but evidence for other modalities, architectures (e.g., transformers), or larger scales is absent.

Key methodological choices lack ablation or sensitivity analysis in the main text: the Hint weighting C (only uniform default is used, plus one ad-hoc zero-except-last configuration in Fig. 6), number of functional Hint terms (Fig. 11 touches on this), and the norm-scaling term. It is unclear how robust the conclusions are to these hyperparameters.

No error bars, seeds, or statistical testing are reported anywhere, despite differences between methods in several figures (e.g., Fig. 9, Fig. 10 self-accuracy) being small; claims like 'FuLA emerges as the most effective' would benefit from significance analysis.
Comparison with representational similarity baselines is thin (only CKA at one point in Sec. 3.1), so the claimed advantage over the broader similarity-metric landscape is not well established.

Presentation has rough edges: Figure 1 and its caption are difficult to follow, several figures are unreadably dense (Figs. 4, 8, 10), and there are typos ('swallow-level', 'lack to ground truth') that suggest insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly motivates a real conceptual gap: standard model stitching probes only forward compatibility, which conflates reliance on different information cues and permits exploitation of previously unseen shortcuts. The proposed forward–backward compatibility requirement is a principled response, well grounded in the invariance literature (Nanda et al., 2022; Feather et al., 2023).

The empirical program is thorough: multiple stitching objectives (HLM, SLM, DM, and the newly proposed FuLA latent-alignment objective), multiple architectures (ResNet-18, VGG-16, ViT-Tiny, ViT-Base), multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, LS-ImageNet-10, ImageNet-100), three random seeds, and controlled manipulations of shortcut availability. The main findings generalize across these settings per the appendix.

Good experimental hygiene: identical initialization schemes across standard and invariance-aware stitching, dedicated sanity checks on the quality of the constructed IRI datasets (App. F.1), explicit control for the data-augmentation confound, and an acknowledged and investigated sanity-check failure for ViT-Base (App. F.2).

The revisiting of the robust vs. non-robust stitching result of Balogh & Jelasity (2023) is a concrete, meaningful demonstration that the new protocol overturns a previously published conclusion, which strengthens the paper's significance beyond methodology alone.

The paper is well written, with a clear toy example (Fig. 1), careful notation, an honest limitations discussion (no oracle ground truth for functional similarity; restriction to image classification), and publicly available code.
weaknesses: The central claims rest on the assumption that optimizing the stitching layer on D_train achieves the unique optimal forward compatibility on D_test, and that the relaxed IRI construction (tolerance ρ, 200 optimization steps) faithfully approximates exact identically represented inputs. The evidence for this is indirect (App. F.1 sanity checks), and the paper itself reports noticeable divergence for ImageNet-100 and a failed sanity check for ViT-Base under SLM, which weakens confidence that all observed invariance-aware drops reflect genuine invariance mismatches rather than artifacts of the IRI construction.

Evaluation is largely qualitative: the paper concedes there is no objective measure of meaningfulness and relies on 'sanity checks grounded on intuitive expectations.' Consequently, claims such as 'more principled' or 'more meaningful' are supported by plausibility arguments rather than by quantitative validation against ground truth, and no quantitative summary statistics (e.g., variance across the three seeds, error bars) are reported for the figures.

There is no clear recommendation on which invariance-enabling formulation is best; the trade-off analysis (Sec. 3.4) shows formulation ranking is architecture-dependent, and SLM retains substantial shortcut exploitation while DM underestimates similarity. A practitioner adopting the method is left without a definitive protocol.

The key failure modes being mitigated were already identified by Smith et al. (2025) for HLM; the paper's main originality is showing the failure generalizes to other forward-compatibility formulations and that IRIs-based training mitigates it. This is a useful but somewhat incremental advance over the prior critique.

The asymmetry in treatment (batch-norm statistics updated for standard stitching but frozen for invariance-aware stitching; augmentation on vs. off) introduces procedural differences between the compared regimes; although the authors report the augmentation confound was controlled, the batch-statistics asymmetry is not explicitly controlled.

The scope is limited to image classification with affine stitching layers and equal-depth stitching (i = j); the generality of forward–backward compatibility to other modalities, tasks, and stitch configurations remains untested, as acknowledged in the limitations.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: recent work (Smith et al., 2025; Balogh & Jelasity, 2025) has shown that forward-only model stitching can be misleading as a functional similarity measure, and the proposed forward-backward compatibility requirement via identically represented inputs (IRIs) is a sensible and novel operationalization of probing invariances within the stitching framework.

The empirical study is unusually comprehensive: four architectures (ResNet-18, VGG-16, ViT-Tiny, ViT-Base), three datasets (CIFAR-10, LS-ImageNet-10, ImageNet-100), multiple alignment objectives (HLM, SLM, DM, and the new FuLA), controlled shortcut-availability conditions, and robust/non-robust model configurations, with three random seeds per configuration.

The authors include dedicated sanity checks (identical-model stitching on D_IRIs, App. F.1) to verify that the relaxed IRI construction preserves stitch-level semantics, and honestly report where these checks partially fail (ViT-Base/ImageNet-100 identity configuration).

The new FuLA objective is a reasonable contribution, interpolating between stitch-level (DM) and output-level (SLM/HLM) forward compatibility, and the analysis of the supervision-strength trade-off (Sec. 3.4) is a genuinely informative observation about the space of stitching formulations.
The limitation that no 'oracle' notion of functional similarity exists, and that evaluation rests on sanity checks, is candidly acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The central claims are validated almost entirely through qualitative 'sanity checks grounded on intuitive expectations' rather than any quantitative ground truth. The paper concedes that definitive conclusions about which setting most faithfully reflects similarity remain out of reach; as a result, the headline claim that invariance-aware stitching is 'more principled' rests on the authors' own intuition being accepted as the reference standard.

The forward-backward compatibility requirement is informal: it relies on an unverified assumption that optimizing the stitching layer on D_train achieves the unique optimal forward compatibility on D_test, and the relaxed IRI set (rho > 0) breaks the exactness of the theoretical requirement, further muddying the interpretation of deviations.

There is a methodological confound between standard and invariance-aware settings: data augmentation is used for standard stitching but turned off for invariance-aware stitching. The authors assert controlling for augmentation 'had minimal effect', but the supporting evidence is not presented in the manuscript.

Reported results include a failed sanity check (SLM fails on the trivial identity-stitching configuration for ViT-Base on ImageNet-100, App. F.2) and erratic SLM behavior under adversarial alignment (Sec. 3.3), which the paper attributes to the formulation rather than to the invariance-aware procedure itself, but this weakens confidence that the method is reliable out of the box.

The novelty is moderate: the core idea (evaluating representations on invariance-inducing metamers) is adapted from Nanda et al. (2022) and Jones et al. (2022) into the stitching framework, and FuLA is a natural application of fitnets-style hints; the contribution is primarily a careful empirical synthesis rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The scope is confined to image classification with modest-scale models, and the practical utility of the metric to practitioners outside the model-similarity literature is not demonstrated (no downstream task uses the similarity measure).

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a concrete, documented failure of standard model stitching (blindness to invariance properties, per Smith et al. 2025) and shows theoretically-appealing reasoning for why forward-only compatibility obscures functional discrepancies (Fig. 1 toy example, forward–backward compatibility requirement).

The proposed invariance-aware stitching, operationalized via identically represented inputs (IRIs), is a natural but non-obvious extension that jointly probes forward and backward compatibility; the new FuLA (functional latent alignment) objective is a sensible intermediate between stitch-level (DM) and output-level (SLM/HLM) formulations.

Empirically thorough: results span CIFAR-10, LS-ImageNet-10, and ImageNet-100 with ResNet-18, VGG-16, ViT-Tiny, and ViT-Base; the paper revisits two published failure modes (models relying on different cues, exploitation of previously unseen predictive cues) and shows both generalize beyond HLM to all forward-only formulations and are mitigated by the invariance-aware setting.

Good self-critical hygiene: the authors include sanity checks for their own methodology (identical stitching with D_IRIs vs D_train, App. F.1), report cases where their setup fails (SLM failing the identity sanity check on ViT-Base, Fig. 11; SLM degeneracy under adversarial alignment), and honestly discuss the absence of an 'oracle' notion of similarity and the restriction to image classification.

Reproducibility is strong: code is released, training and stitching hyperparameters are fully specified (App. B), the agreement probability metric and IRI construction are precisely defined, and experiments average over three seeds.

The robust vs. non-robust revisit (Sec. 3.3) yields a genuinely new, publication-worthy insight: robust models show consistently higher functional convergence under invariance-aware stitching, corroborating Jones et al. (2022) via a functional rather than representational lens.
weaknesses: The central claim that invariance-aware stitching is 'more principled' rests on intuitive sanity checks rather than any objective validation; there is a risk of circularity, since the method penalizes models with non-shared invariances by construction, so the cross-bias result (similarity drops to chance) is partly baked in rather than independently discovered.

Several method-selection questions remain unresolved: the paper concludes there is 'no clear winner' among invariance-enabling formulations, with SLM exhibiting erratic/degenerate behavior in some configurations and an acknowledged sanity-check failure for ViT-Base identity stitching; practical guidance for practitioners choosing a formulation is therefore weak.

The key assumption that optimizing the stitching layer on D_train yields unique optimal forward compatibility on D_test (underpinning the interpretation of deviations as backward-incompatibility) is asserted rather than verified, and could be violated for hard-to-align model pairs.

Computational cost of the method is underexplored: constructing IRIs requires ~200 optimization steps per sample per stitch level and per front model, which scales poorly relative to standard stitching; no cost comparison is provided.

Scope is limited to image classification with a single stitching-layer family (1×1 conv / linear); whether the forward–backward compatibility framing transfers to other modalities or more expressive alignment families is left to future work.

The 'excessive agreement probability' metric (difference between pixel-injected and pixel-permuted splits) is somewhat ad hoc, and its sensitivity to the specific shortcut construction is not analyzed.
